title: Never Ship a Known Critical Error
intro: A team decided to ship “save content blocks” without edit or delete, because the stack couldn't support them yet. They called it MVP.

topics.title: Never Ship a Known Critical Error

learn.title: Why it was critical, not minor
learn.text:
Users would be stuck with every typo forever. Blocks could only be removed by an admin.

• Typos saved permanently
• Workspaces clogged with stale, slightly different blocks
• “I have to email an admin to delete this?”

A **critical error** stops users completing the task or recovering from a mistake — different from friction.

try.q: What distinguishes a critical error from friction?
options: It has no workaround in the UI
try.explain: Friction slows people down; a critical error stops them.

left.label: What the team saw
items: Fix it in a later release

learn.title: One-on-one persuasion failed
learn.text:
The argument that it still met MVP criteria “received no pushback in the meeting”.

The designer wasn't convinced and felt their concern had been dismissed. Calabro's attempts to argue it in conversation didn't change anything either.

Resistance here was about ownership and deadlines, not about the evidence.

try.q: What was the real source of the resistance?
try.explain: Which is why arguing the evidence one-on-one didn't work.

learn.title: What changed it
learn.text:
He teamed up with the designer, prototyped the feature quickly, and ran a short usability test with **five users**.

One participant spent several minutes trying to remove a block they had saved by mistake.

They cut a **two-minute highlight reel** of people hitting dead ends. That changed the outcome.

The lasting fix: make “no known critical errors at launch” an explicit release criterion.

options: A short highlight reel of users failing
try.explain: Five users, a quick prototype, two minutes of footage.

test.q: What was missing from the feature?
test.explain: Users could save blocks but never change them.

test.q: What does “MVP” not justify, according to this article?
test.explain: It's a release blocker, not a trade-off.

test.q: How many users were in the test?
test.explain: Enough to produce footage nobody could argue with.

test.q: What is the lasting fix he recommends?
options: Make it an explicit release criterion
Require research sign-off on every release
Add a UX representative to planning
Run a usability test before each launch
test.explain: “No known critical errors at launch”, written down.

test.q: Why does showing beat arguing here?
options: Footage of users failing is hard to dispute
Video is more persuasive than data
It avoids naming who was wrong
test.explain: The evidence stopped being a matter of opinion.
